No one who has any understanding of the Canada of today could possibly believe that constitutional change made in Britain, by the British, on our behalf could be conceived by the majority of Canadians as being anything else but illegitimate. A made-in-Britain constitution will never be accepted by Canadians.
Several speakers on behalf of the government position have taken a very critical view of the so-called Vancouver amending formula, claiming that it would impose or lead to a checkerboard or patchwork crazy-quilt pattern in Canada. As my colleague the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) pointed out in his speech of February 18, 1981, that observation is simply nonsensical. As the member for Rosedale indicated in his speech, we already have a patchwork or a checkerboard system in Canada. In 1867 the British North America Act established a checkerboard pattern. Section 92 of the BNA Act laid out provincial powers and provided that the provinces could do with them as they saw fit. In other words, the provinces could create a checkerboard pattern, and that has been the pattern in Canada for 114 years. Section 133 imposed conditions on Quebec by which other provinces were not affected. This proposal is a patchwork. We have been a checkerboard or patchwork quilt since confederation. Far from weakening Canada, this has contributed to uniting the country and making it strong.
Perhaps the most maddening aspect of this non-thinking criticism of the Vancouver formula is the fundamental dishonesty of the government's position, since the very proposal that it is now attempting to force upon the country will itself create a checkerboard. Whereas heretofore, at least since 1930, every province in Canada was equal, under the Victoria formula proposed by the government there will be perhaps as many as four classes of provinces, certainly three. This is a concept wholly unacceptable to those lower-class provinces and clearly unacceptable to the vast majority of fair-minded Canadians.
It is the contention of the Prime Minister's apologists that a provision allowing provinces to opt out of constitutional amendments unacceptable to a province will somehow, through this patchwork or crazy-quilt pattern which might result, end up in Canada being a lesser country. In proposing
that position, these apologists show an abysmal ignorance both of the nature of Canada and of the nature of federal democratic countries around the world.
Is Switzerland any less a united federal state because it has five official languages and because the cantons or provinces are autonomous to the point that citizenship itself is actually granted by the canton and not by the central government? Is West Germany any less a united federal state because the border guards are members of the lander or provincial police forces rather than officers of the central government? Is the United States any less united as a result of the patchwork which results from each state having a different criminal code?
Is it not just possible that this patchwork in virtually every other federal democratic state on this planet is the very characteristic that creates unity in those federal countries as opposed to disunity? Even unitary states, such as the United Kingdom, have a wide variety of different regional or local governments and laws. The Isle of Man, which has been part of the United Kingdom for centuries, has its own separate parliament totally different from Westminster and totally different in character from the parliament of Northern Ireland and the parliaments of Scotland and Wales. The civil code in Scotland is different from that in England. Evidence from around the world overwhelmingly points to the fact that a patchwork or a crazy-quilt pattern, to use the government's phrase, is not only common but may be essential to the maintenance of a unified country.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in comparing Canada to other federal states in the democratic world, the distinguishing feature about Canada is not that there is a crazy-quilt or checkerboard pattern but that there is very little or comparatively little difference across the country. The most serious difference and the difference which I think contributes most to the disunity of the country is that Canada alone among the federal states lacks any provincial or regional representation in the central government. Canada alone is attempting to maintain a national or federal government that is unitary in nature.
That is the real tragedy of what the Prime Minister is doing. The over-all thrust of the constitutional proposal is to make our government even more unitary in nature than it already is, whereas the crying need is for constitutional amendments that will recognize the federal nature of the country. It is interesting and sad to note that the one member of the cabinet who recognizes this fact through his chairmanship of the task force on national unity, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), has been utterly excluded from any participation in the current debate.
The Prime Minister simply does not know this country. He views Canada as Peter Newman, the editor of Maclean's, once observed, as basically consisting of Upper Canada, Lower Canada and outer Canada. He views Canada as a family formed by the marriage of Upper and Lower Canada, with the remaining provinces being the progeny or children of the marriage. To him we are all a family, but the parents must remain dominant and the children subservient or second class. What the Prime Minister does not recognize is that that model
March 16, 1981

does not and will not fit Canada. It will never be accepted by outer Canadians. Canadians in my province and in the other western provinces are saying, "Please let us be first-class Canadians; let us count to the same extent as other Canadians."
Hear, hear!

That is what is wrong with the government's proposed Victoria formula. It would encase in a Constitution, in perpetuity, a second-class status, if not a third-class status, for my province and for other provinces that make up outer Canada. I plead with the members of the government to stop and consider what they might be doing. To paraphrase Sir John A. Macdonald, if you treat people with respect, they will act as free people generally do; call them a faction and they will become factious. Impose this totally unacceptable amending formula on Canadians and you will weaken forever their commitment to Canada.
One of the personal disappointments to me in this constitutional debate has been the attitude and position taken by members of the government party who represent francophone constituencies. On many occasions since I have been a member I have heard francophone members pleading in this House, not in a subservient way but in a plaintive way, for an understanding of the fears and aspirations of Canada's French-speaking citizens. Many times I have heard members saying, in essence, that what they wanted was changes in Canada's federation that would give French-speaking Canadians the dignity, the opportunity and the respect due a first-class citizen.
I remember in particular the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve not too many years ago arguing on behalf of French-speaking air traffic controllers that they be allowed to use their language and that French-speaking Canadians be allowed to fly aeroplanes and communicate with the ground in their language, because as Canadians they felt that they had a right to the same privileges, the same courtesies, the same status, as English-speaking Canadians.
One would like to think that people who have gone through that kind of personal experience would therefore be sensitive to, and aware of, similar calls for respect and equality from other Canadians. Yet today, with western Canadians in the thousands turning out to West-Fed and other meetings making basically the same plea, for understanding and for first-class status, these members turn a deaf ear. It is particularly disappointing that the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maison-neuve should adopt that attitude since I was led to believe he was more sensitive and more principled. It is sad to see members opposite, who have gone through what at times must have been a humiliating experience trying to get first-class status for their constituents and other French-speaking Canadians, turn around and be so damned insensitive to similar concerns for first-class status from other Canadians, be they from the west or the Atlantic region.
The Constitution
Perhaps I am being naive in assuming that fair play or sensitivity to the aspirations of fellow Canadians matter a whit. Perhaps all that matters is power, and since fate or the unfolding universe has given the Prime Minister the power he now possesses, that he will use that power to impose his model of Canada on the nation no matter that that model does not fit.
Even more disturbing to fair-minded Canadians than the Victoria formula is the provision for constitutional amendment by so-called referendum. The use of referenda is provided for in the constitutions of a number of democratic federal states, such as Switzerland and the United States. In both of these countries the axiom is that sovereign power rests ultimately with the people, and because of this the initiation of a referendum is built into their federalisms. In both of these federal states referenda can be initiated by either the state or the people and the results are binding.
As George Woodcock points out in a November, 1980, article in Saturday Night magazine: '
This is quite different from our (Canadian) politicians' gambits which are really plebiscites such as Levesque's referendum on sovereignty-association or Trudeau's proposed vote on the Constitution, devised merely to gain endorsement from what the leaders have devised. (Hitler was an expert on this kind of popular vote.)
As Mr. Woodcock has accurately observed, this referendum proposal is nothing more or less than a tool whereby the Prime Minister could impose constitutional change upon the country. With the right of initiation resting with government, with the ability to state the question and to set the rules, the cards are clearly overwhelmingly stacked in favour of the federal government, or, in other words, the Prime Minister. What George Woodcock points out is more closely analogous to the procedures in Hitler's Germany than to the referendum procedures in truly democratic federal states.
Oh, oh!

If members opposite find George Woodcock's words unacceptable, I might refer them to an article by Michael Valpy in the October 8 Vancouver Sun where he examined the use of referenda similar to this in other countries. He stated:
In France in 1958, against a backdrop of political stalemate and unstable government, a referendum gave Charles de Gaulle the powers of a near-dictator.
Is it a coincidence that in late November, 1979, after announcing his retirement, the Prime Minister should give a speech to the University of Montreal saying that his preference for Canada is a presidential system based on the French model? Is that just a coincidence? Mr. Valpy continued:
In Germany in 1934, against a backdrop of Nazi-fostered fear, severe economic disorder, and street fighting between political extremists, a referendum gave Adolf Hitler unchecked executive power.
In Canada in 1944, against a backdrop of sincere and principled political division between Canadians over overseas war service, a referendum-backed in English Canada, rejected in French Canada-gave a timid central government the courage to impose conscription. It also left a legacy of hate and bigotry that might have been avoided by a political act of leadership that sidestepped spelling out the nation's naked differences-

March 16, 1981
The Constitution
Backed by Martin Goldfarb and millions of advertising dollars, it would give Ottawa an incredible whiphand.
A government that was truly democratic and that understood the federal nature of this country would not put forward referenda procedures of this sort, the type used by Hitler and de Gaulle. If it was interested in referenda, it would put forward the sort employed by other democracies, such as Switzerland and the United States. I might also point out to the House that, while not using the same dramatic analogies as Mr. Valpy or Mr. Woodcock, Mr. Gordon Robertson, former clerk of the privy council and an adviser to the Prime Minister on the Constitution, has made the same observation about Section 42 of the proposed Constitution.
1 have not in my remarks directed much attention to the proposed charter of rights, not because I do not believe it is important but rather because many other speakers on our side, and in particular the hon. member for Provencher, have made excellent and perceptive observations in regard to it. I would only say that, along with the vast majority in the House, I believe the addition of the charter of rights to the Canadian Constitution would be a positive step. But along with the vast majority of fair-minded Canadians, I also strongly believe that it is absolutely immoral to have the British impose this charter of rights. A charter of rights should be examined here in Canada by Canadians, and it should only be after the very closest of examination and only after very, very extensive public debate here in Canada that a charter should be put into the Constitution. This proposed charter is at the moment very imperfect in many ways, and we would be doing the country a great disservice if we locked in this imperfect charter.
In committee the members of the New Democratic Party moved 43 amendments. They found 43 things wrong with this charter of rights. Two of the amendments were passed, which means they still find 41 things wrong. Why are they so quick to vote for this charter which to their minds is so imperfect?
It seems so fundamental that it is almost trite to say this, but it must be said because of its omission from the charter of rights. A charter, to mean anything, must contain an acknowledgement of the supremacy of God in order to demonstrate that rights do not come from man or from some leader; rights are ours because we are human beings created in the image of God. For the government not to accept that particular amendment is, to me, a glaring and unacceptable omission.
A charter of rights without property rights is absurd. Property rights are absolutely fundamental to human rights. My family background is not dissimilar to that of a lot of western Canadians. My grandparents came to this country from eastern Europe prior to the turn of the last century. Then, as now, the state owned and controlled all land and property, and by that simple expedient controlled all rights; individuals had none. My grandparents came to this country because of the opportunity to own land, to have the economic freedom that comes from that, because all other rights are meaningless without economic rights. Without property rights, economic
rights can never be assured. How anybody could propose a charter of rights without property rights is beyond me. The socialists obviously do not believe in property rights because they do not believe in that kind of freedom.
Let us have a charter of rights, Mr. Speaker, but one made in Canada by Canadians, including the acknowledgement of the supremacy of God and property rights. It is hard to pick up a magazine or newspaper that does not have an observation by someone whose opinion should be respected, pointing out some imperfection in these rights. How can we so quickly and glibly jam through this clearly imperfect proposal and hustle it off to Britain to have it imposed on us by the British? This charter, Mr. Speaker, was basically designed on the back of an envelope by various special interest groups who came before the committee and bargained for support with the minister.
I conclude by saying that I am extremely concerned about the impact of this proposal on my part of Canada. The people in western Canada want to be first-class Canadians but they feel they are being forced into a second-class status in perpetuity by the headlong push of this government. Unless stopped, this government and their sheep will be doing irreparable damage to this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, welcome this opportunity to add my comments on the constitutional proposals before the House. Before I get into the main part of my speech, I want to comment on some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) during his 40-minute discussion of constitutional reform.
Not only members of the opposition but constituents of mine want to understand why we are, in 1981, about to embark on this path of constitutional reform. I have been here only one year and some days, but I think it is safe to say that for all of us the results of the referendum last May 20 were gratifying, regardless of party affiliation. When someone says to me, as did the hon. member for Calgary Centre, that according to a Gallup poll 64 per cent of Canadians are against unilateral patriation, you could put the same question, if you worded it in the way Gallup did, to the members on this side of the House and probably have 64 per cent of us say that we do not want to move in a unilateral way. But that is not the simple issue involved here.
Last June, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) began the summer trial with his provincial counterparts in preparation for the September conference, we all wished in our hearts that the conference would work. It would have been much better had the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) been able to arrive at a package for constitutional reform by consensus, but that is not the way it was to be. As was evident in the September conference, there was a breakdown and that left the government in the position of having to decide how best to go about constitutional reform and how best to achieve support for this package.
I think it is fair to say that the joint committee proposal before us represents to the best of our ability as parliamentari-
March 16, 1981

ans a charter of rights, a statement of belief in the need for patriation with an amending formula, one that is as acceptable as it can be to a majority of Canadians. The government has gone completely out of its way to accommodate everybody in the sense that there were 12 items under discussion at the September conference. The government made a conscious decision to go with the least number of proposals that would antagonize the least number of Canadians.
That is the proposal we gave to the joint committee in October of last year, and to have the hon. member for Calgary Centre say at this late stage in the debate that we are attempting to jam down the throats of Canadians a Constitution that nobody else wants I think belies the fact that a great deal of work was done by the joint committee, by all members of this House for five long months. 1 commend them for their work in that committee, and I think, quite frankly, we have before us proposals that will go a long way toward addressing the problems that have existed here in Canada since 1867.
That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the main point of my address. I want to come back to this theme throughout, and that is that we are about to embark upon a path that began in 1867 and along which there is still unfinished business to attend to. I would like to point out that when this House passes the joint resolution and presents it to Westminster, it does not mean that the process has ended. It is the beginnning of a new constitutional process; there is still unfinished business to attend to in this nation.
The year 1867 saw the birth of a new nation, a northern nationality, and as history recorded 50 years later war gave us an identity. Nova Scotians and Albertans, the soldiers of 1914, came home in 1919 as Canadians. In 1931, through the passage of the Statute of Westminster, we secured tangible autonomy in that no statute or law of Canada could be ruled invalid simply because it was repugnant to the law of the United Kingdom, save and except with regard to the BNA Act. I repeat, save and except the BNA Act. That is why I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House that there is unfinished business to attend to.
I call to the attention of all members the words of one of Montreal's great men of letters, F. R. Scott, who said:
We have a rendez-vous with the BNA Act. It's going to come some day.
Well, it is now 1981 and this is the prophesied day. We have at this time reflected on and debated at length our constitutional future. We must now act to bring the Constitution home, secure in the knowledge that our children and their children will enjoy their country in the future, safe in the fact that no other nation or state has the power or legislative authority to change our fundamental laws.
That is what is ultimately meant by the term "responsible self-government", and it is long overdue, too long unfinished. Never before have we had so clearly the opportunity, albeit moved by its own passions and standards, to advance the civic culture of Canada, to unveil to the world what the ideals of Canadian society stand for, but most importantly, to decide for ourselves what it means to be Canadian.
The Constitution
If the process to date has been difficult-and perhaps it will become more difficult yet-that is as it should be. All great social reform requires it. This government believes that it must now, in 1981, move on constitutional reform, not because some constituent assembly has ordained it, not because some community of communities commands it and not because some premiers have made deals, but because Canadians will always feel inadequate and unsure of their identity until someone determines for their well-being a definition of what it means to be a Canadian.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
We will act because this government knows that Canadians have that capacity. We have been disabled far too long. For ourselves and for Canada let us decide to throw away the crutch and stand on guard for our country, able at last, but by no means least, to amend our own Constitution.
Detractors of all varieties would have us believe that Canada is about to be rent apart by actions of this government to patriate our Constitution and by refusing, as the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has suggested, to take into account the larger interests of Canada. I do not know anything of these larger interests to which the right hon. member refers. If there is some kind of other directed national interest, then we in the government believe, even at this late stage, that the right hon. member is again afforded another opportunity to share his views with his fellow Canadians. We look forward to the right hon. member's positive recommendations, not to thwart constitutional evolution in this country, but to participate affirmatively in its making. We recognize the right to oppose. Constructive criticisms are the energizing force in this debate. We are thankful to the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) who, I am sure, shares the conviction, which transcends politics, that we must all get on with the job.
The age of technology presents us with the reality that we are all participators in the cult of innovation. This technological imperative alone dictates that our fundamental law must change. Because of this debate and the constitutional process the law itself is being changed. Great new institutions are being founded privately, and whole new networks of existing contractual relations are being renewed in a thousand ways.
The legislative reform this government is proposing is embedded in these broader, voluntary and private formal and informal modifications of Canadian society which our new Constitution will serve to consolidate and provide a new framework for Canada for ever new departures. In short, we have the opportunity to enjoy the change that constitutional reform can bring.

Mr. Speaker, if some members do not feel it advisable to have a Constitution which may be amended in Canada, then we must recognize that our cultural policy is threatened. I personally consider Canada to be a nation-state made up of

March 16, 1981
The Constitution
various cultural and language groups, and which expects to find in the Constitution a definition of the rights and powers of individuals and of political institutions. If that aim is overshadowed by other considerations, it means that we do not have the collective will to assume our responsibilities and control our destiny. I, for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that after 54 years of unsuccessful attempts, it is high time we patriated our Constitution.

Not all constitutional benchmarks in democratic history are the product of seemingly endless negotiations. This begs the question so adroitly raised by the Prime Minister: If Parliament's decisions must be negotiated, how can they be decisions? Do they not simply become negotiating positions?
Some benchmarks are accomplished by deliberate action supported by the greatest number of people of good will. The BNA Act was the result of such an affirmation. Its concluding chapter can be as well. The opportunity cost of such unfinished business is too great. I for one do not wish to be associated any longer with Canada's constitutional predicament-our inability to amend, on our own recognizance, our basic laws. That fate leaves an aversionary taste. Not to respond at this juncture in our history to the imperative before us suggests a profound cynicism about our own competence. It attracts and invites mastheads in our national and local papers which predisposes or forces some members of this House to talk of political warfare.
I believe, as do a great many Canadians, that nothing could be further from the truth. The only reason for discord is that we simply have not been able to agree on a method to be written into our documentary Constitution which allows full expression to the term "sovereignty of Canada". In short, we shall not be fully sovereign or fulfilled as Canadians until the parliament of the United Kingdom is no longer the only recourse for amending the Constitution.
I have heard this often from speakers who have spoken before me in this debate. The hon. member for Calgary Centre spoke about the need for some further perfection of the charter of rights which is presently before this House. This is the same member who six months ago stood up in this House and said that Canadians simply wanted their Constitution patriated. He was totally against having an amending formula. Now I hear discussions about what kind of an amending formula it should be. Now I hear from hon. members opposite that we have not gone far enough in certain areas of the charter of rights.
Weren't you here on October 22?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Don't worry about him.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
I am not worried about the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Now I hear from other hon. members on the benches opposite that certain rights in the charter of rights do not go far enough. There has been quite a change in the last six months.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre also said that there are certain inalienable rights every Canadian should enjoy.
Yet his own party says that the charter of rights should have an opting out formula. He properly pointed out that under the existing BNA Act there has been some checkerboard effect in this country. We have allowed the provinces to opt out with respect to certain taxation powers. We have always had that flexibility in our Constitution, but can we afford to allow provinces to opt out with respect to the inalienable rights of our citizens? Either there will be basic rights enjoyed by every citizen in this country regardless of his place of residence, or we no longer will have a nation by anyone's definition. If there are to be basic rights, they belong to all Canadians, and provinces should not be allowed to opt out of the principles expressed in the charter of rights.
While we all recognize that words are sometimes inadequate vehicles to convey ideas and that intensity of feeling rather than substance is the order of the day, I believe we have dwelt too much upon the process of constitutional reform and have not addressed ourselves enough to the content of constitutional reform.
I do not wish to dwell at length on the issue of the amending formula, save to say that without one which is fair and equitable, both rigid and flexible, and cognizant of our federal character, our definition of a truly federal state falls short of the mark. All constitutional authorities agree that the provincial legislatures have the right to amend their constitution as it affects them, save with regard to the offices of lieutenant governors. Yet Canada's national legislature cannot do so at its own discretion without the consent of the parliament of Great Britain. Thus, Canada is relegated to being the only free nation in the world which is not at liberty to change its Constitution without the consent of another sovereign state. For any province, court of appeal or person to suggest that this government's proposed Canada Act, Constitution Act and the patriation instruments are in themselves unconstitutional is inappropriate, in that such a view or judgment serves only to suborn the right of this central government to act.
I need not remind the House that those who argue for unanimity on the issue of patriation of the Constitution do not and cannot guarantee the perfection of what will be achieved. I suggest that even if all 11 governments were to concur in the method of patriation at this time, there is no guarantee that a perfect instrument will be obtained. This is why our resolution calls for an amending formula and a method to find one to assure that our system of government will be based on a set of laws and not on the whims of men. No member of this House has higher authority than that which is transferred by the electorate.
The puppet on the provincial shoestring approach of the official opposition, which argues for opting out and against a national referendum for breaking a deadlock should no amending protocol be found, is, to me, lamentable. The important and, indeed, crucial test of the legitimacy of this government's actions will be determined by what we do with the Constitution when we get it back. If an amending formula is not achieved, the federal government reserves the exclusive right
March 16, 1981

to take the issue of a formula to the people in the form of a national referendum.
I, for one, must believe that the wit, the intelligence and the desire of the premiers and the Prime Minister to build an amending formula worthy of the status of Canada can be accomplished within two years. That is the challenge before us. It seems only logical that if we, as legislators here and in the provinces, cannot resolve this impasse at the end of 24 months of concerted effort, recourse to the population at large is the only solution. I cannot see how some hon. members in the opposition benches can argue that a referendum will thwart the democratic process. At the very least, the opportunity for the people of Canada to decide is not only the opportunity to renew the social contract but to exercise the highest privilege democracy affords.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We have never argued against that.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary Centre said just now that a referendum would tear this country apart.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You misunderstood his remark.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
You are misunderstanding mine.
I would remind the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues that when politicians fail to break an impasse, it is best to go to the people, because then we have recourse to our biggest resource, what prime minister Sir Robert Borden once referred to as "the commonplace quality of common sense." It therefore strikes me that any legislation must absolutely exercise and preserve a balance between complexity and conscience. I believe that principle is clearly contained in this government's constitutional proposals.
The federal government holds relentlessly to the conviction that there are certain basic rights inherent in and crucial to Canadian citizenship and Canadians' way of life. That is why we maintain that these rights must be entrenched in the Constitution as a charter of rights. Because of the virtue of these rights, the positive and negative notions of freedoms- freedom to and freedom from-would be standardized and universally applied, and once entrenched would make Canada a free, model society for the rest of the world to emulate. That is why we argue for constitutional provisions to prohibit provincial or federal government interference, as this is necessary to guarantee the privacy of individual rights.
I too, like Gordon Fairweather, our Human Rights Commissioner, am anxious for an entrenched bill of rights. While it is certain that some rights require more protection, it is not this aspect which I personally find exciting. An entrenched charter of rights and freedoms is much more-it is a testament to the human spirit, a guide on how to live and grow in our humanity. All manners of excellence that we accept for our guidance, and all obligations to which we grant jurisdiction over us, can be defined by our respect for human greatness. As a statement
The Constitution
of objects of our respect, a charter of rights and freedoms allows us to pass on continuously a rich inheritance for the as yet unborn Canadians for all time. In essence, such a charter codifies a standard of conduct between all men. A charter of rights is a statement of universal intent. The proposed charter will serve to make Canadians understood as a people and as a nation which realizes that the freedom of the subjective person to do as he pleases is overruled by the freedom of the responsible person to act as he or she must.
Even the most intimate rights of the individual Canadian cannot be enforced against the state without the corresponding judicial protection that entrenching in the Constitution would provide. It is the view of this government that the Constitution is the best place in which to provide for the protection of our freedoms. The members of this government concur with the thinking that civilization in part is measured by the willingness of those who have power to yield it up to third parties for adjudication.
The charter will accomplish much for us, but it will also tell us how others see and understand Canadians. In short, it will do much to reinforce our sense of national identity. I know one myth that it will dispel forever: never again will confederation be called the graveyard of minorities.
I return to my theme of unfinished business. I believe there are compelling reasons why we must move forward quickly at this stage of debate. I refer to a rather generally held belief, one held too long, that the present federal Constitution has much to do with the intractable problems of regional economic development and disparities. Surely all members of the House must realize that there is no alternative to our market system which can support our economic interests without threatening our personal freedom as individual Canadians. What is required is action by this government to establish and maintain an economic environment in which the market can best perform its essential function. Financial aggression on the part of one province which argues against mobility rights does nothing but serve to further institutionalize disparities in another province perhaps less fortunate in its natural endowments. The demand for greater provincial autonomy at this time only inhibits the development of a national economic strategy.
We are not proposing to put something over on the provinces. A statement made recently by my colleague, the Minister of Justice, offers instruction. He said:
We do not want to restrict the ability of the provincial governments to deal with social, cultural and economic issues within their jurisdiction; but we want to ensure that the required laws, regulations and practices do not discriminate against Canadians from other provinces. Such discrimination goes against the principle of economic union and creates internal barriers which go against a fundamental principle of nationhood.
By entrenching such a value in the Constitution, we are not proposing change for the sake of change, nor imposing a value that is academic. Rather, we are saying to the average Canadian that she or he has a basic constitutional right to economic security wherever it may be obtained in this country.
The constitutional reform proposal before the House essentially addresses the question of sharing our wealth to make

March 16, 1981
The Constitution
Canada work as it can, for it is vital that all Canadians enjoy a national standard of material well-being. To that end, Mr. Speaker, Part 1, Section 6 of the Constitution Act provides every citizen of Canada with three basic economic rights. These are, first, the right to enter, remain in, and leave Canada; second, that every citizen and every permanent resident of Canada have the right to move from province to province and to take up residence; and third, the right of every Canadian to seek gainful employment without hindrance. These rights cannot be conditional or discriminatory in relation to a person's previous province of residence. Anything less means that a Canadian citizen would have his basic citizenship right embargoed by the unilateral action of a province.
In the recent past we have seen examples of construction workers not being allowed to work in a province where work was to be found. The first premier of Newfoundland believed in the concept of mobility rights, but the present leadership in Newfoundland does not support it.
Entrenching mobility rights and ensuring the free flow of capital does nothing to ruin federalism, as some members of the opposition have argued. Rather, it actualizes the concept. Ill-conceived and poorly erected barriers do not make good neighbours. Instead, discriminatory practices only serve the creed of those who would beggar thy neighbour. Now more than ever before, Canada must strive to be a country without internal barriers if we are to ensure the prosperity of Canadians and sustain our economic growth.
Mobility rights are principally the cement that holds our economic union together. This is why, Mr. Speaker, the Pepin-Robarts report concluded that reform of the Constitution and of Canada's political institutions would be justified, even if the single purpose was to improve the ability of the Canadian public and private sectors to address themselves to the economic policy requirements of the future. Surely it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that bargaining and negotiation with regard to these matters are rife with difficulties and significant costs.
This government believes that ample time has been provided to work out these issues, yet we have not been able to do so because of lack of agreement and the existence of more than one view of Canada. So in this session of Parliament in the spring of 1981, we have come to a constitutional crossroads. At this moment of history it is true that the Canadian caravan has travelled a long road to nationhood. Perhaps the will of this Parliament will provide us finally with a sovereign, constitutional democracy and, as some of us have longed for and hoped for, with a constitutional regime that can at last help us to cope with our problems and allow us to get on with our national life.
I thought Bruce Hutchinson said it best when he said:
After a hundred years of joint experience we are in a peril from no one but ourselves .. . and we hold in our keeping a trust much larger than we know.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED TAX CREDITS FOR NORTHERN HUNTERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to give income tax credits for the purchase of hunting implements to persons in the Northwest Territories, Labrador and Arctic Quebec who hunt in order to provide a substantial portion of their food supply and whose livelihood is hunting.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today I speak as a hunter and a trapper. I have very legitimate concerns about the financing of the vocations of hunters and trappers.
The outcome of this private member's motion is a foregone conclusion, considering the indication from across the way. However, I am glad to have raised this matter in the House.
Hunting is a legitimate occupation; not a residue of history or a sport. Government should encourage the maintenance of the hunting and trapping sector of our economy for a number of reasons.
First, in the Arctic regions, hunting and trapping make a significant contribution to the local food supply. The Lancaster Sound study of the communities in northern Baffin Island
March 16, 1981

reports that the imputed value of country food available per year is between $568 and $2,173 per capita. The significance of this is exaggerated by the scarcity or non-existence and high cost of nutritionally valuable store-bought goods in northern communities.
Second, hunting and trapping are key factors in the development of a diversified northern economy. A strong renewable resource sector is essential to offset the worst consequences of boom-and-bust non-renewable resource development.
Third, hunting is essential to and is Inuit culture. Dr. Peter J. Usher wrote in an article entitled "Evaluating Country Food in the Northern Native Economy":
Food preferences and habits are an important part of any cultural heritage, and are often very deep-rooted. In a society where hunting is a central tradition, foods have a richness of meaning which stems from their procurement, distribution and preparation, as well as their eating... Country food has nutritional, social and cultural values which cannot be replaced by any substitute and cannot be measured by market criteria or evaluated in cash.
Fourth, it is often assumed that the traditional economy is declining as participation in the wage economy increases, and that this pattern is inevitable and proper. However, hunting and trapping activities in the north are not dying out; their importance in the future economy must be recognized and considered. The maintenance and growth of a healthy and diversified northern economy is not possible without a strong, renewable resource base.
At present, the people of the north are forced into a position of participating in a weak wage economy so that they can afford to hunt. Hunting is so expensive that many people carry a heavy burden of debt throughout most of the year. But, of necessity and as value to their societies, people in Arctic regions are loath to give up this system of harvesting.
I should like to quote a few prices of hunting implements and equipment, since it is quite popular for southern people to quote prices. This information was received from people in Rankin Inlet and Whale Cove in the Keewatin region. For example, the capital cost of a snowmobile is at least $4,000. This is double the 1976 cost. A snowmobile hardly, if ever, lasts for more than one year. It is the best rough terrain vehicle in the world; however, it is the least efficient of gas consumption machines. The cost of material to build a sled in the north costs $400. This also never lasts more than a year. A canoe, which is essential for summer hunting, costs $3,000 including freight. I see on the canal in Ottawa people who have recreational vehicles which are four and five times the prices I am quoting because they are so much better equipment. Hunters in the north would like such equipment, but they cannot afford it.
An outboard motor in the north costs $2,500, that is a small machine, 40-horsepower. A cheap rifle costs $400. We see sports hunters coming from the United States with $2,000 rifles. The hunters in the north would like to own these rifles, but they cannot because they are far too expensive for our financial return. A rifle with a scope costs at least $600. Rope, which is essential to hunting, costs $160, and so on. The prices for all the equipment needed for hunting in the north are
Income Tax
astronomical. They are three and four times what they would be in Ottawa, Winnipeg, Vancouver and so forth.
The prices of hunting equipment have risen astronomically in the last few years. As I said, the price of a snowmobile has doubled since 1976. Because they are in constant use under adverse conditions, a well-maintained snowmobile may last only a couple of seasons. In fact, most last only one season.
The hunter is caught in a vicious economic circle. The only source of monetary income in the traditional economy is derived from the sale of furs, but the price of furs is variable, uncertain, and therefore cannot be depended upon. Most hunters are forced to participate in the wage economy, at least seasonally or part-time, in order to provide the income required to subsidize hunting operations. This situation is complicated by the fact that jobs are not always available.
I would like to point out, as an aside, that while there are 7,000 employees in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, there are 22,000 Inuit. That is a ratio of one bureaucrat to three Inuit. This is pretty deplorable; that money could be usefully used elsewhere. If we consider that there are another 2,000 employees in the territorial government, it means the ratio is 1.5 Inuit to one bureaucrat.
The hunter increasingly finds himself in the position of being dependent upon an unstable wage economy in order to finance his hunting activities, although neither of these activities offers firm monetary rewards. Furthermore, time spent working for wages leaves less time available for hunting and, hence, nutrition.
The strengthening of the hunting and trapping economy in the north, including government recognition of this sector as viable and worthy of support, is necessary in order to break out of this circle of dependency. The cost of nutritionally valuable food in the north is notoriously high when available. As I said, in many communities it is not available. I do not consider dried-out or out-dated pork chops or canned goods as being nutritionally valuable. A reduction in hunting would lead to less nutritious diets and higher costs.
When a community is dependent upon the outside to provide food, it is in a very precarious social and economic position. The insecurity that such dependency breeds destroys the vitality of a community. Steps must be taken to ensure that the hunting economic is not crippled beyond recovery.
I should like to turn now to a brief examination of government support of other sectors of the economy which produce food for Canadian consumption. Tax expenditures on the farming and fishing sectors in 1980 totalled over $100 million. This is small compared to the billions spent on the oil and gas industry. I should like to quote from a document entitled "Government of Canada Tax Expenditure Account". Table 1 refers to the resource sector and reads as follows:
1.	Fast write-off for Canadian exploration expenses.
2.	Fast write-off for Canadian development expenses.
3.	331/3 per cent earned depletion allowance.
This is a total of $1,250 million. However, farmers and Fishermen are able to deduct expenses for tools under $200,

March 16, 1981
Income Tax
gear, gasoline and oil for operating equipment. They are also able to claim a capital cost depreciation allowance on aircraft, automobiles, trucks, boats, outboard motors and sleighs. Hunters are not allowed to claim these expenses, although hunters in outpost camps-and there are very few, possibly three or four in the north-are subsidized by the government of the Northwest Territories. However, hunters in large communities do not have any program to assist them to defray hunting costs. Fishermen and farmers have these types of programs about which I am speaking.
Canada is a major fur-bearing nation. Between 1968 and 1978 our exports in fur products rose 258 per cent, from $35.8 million in 1968 to $128.2 million in 1978. During the same period the trade balance surplus in the fur industry rose from $19 million to $44.4 million. Thus, the export of fur products has increasingly achieved a trade balance surplus while the Canadian economy as a whole is plagued by import deficits in the balance of payments.
Hunters and trappers in the north face a situation where their traditional livelihood is becoming more expensive and difficult to maintain. Incomes received from hunting and trapping hardly reflect the valuable contribution which this sector makes to the Canadian balance of payments. In 1976 per capita income in smaller communities ranged as low as 81 per cent below the Canadian average. Imagine that! Try to buy a new Ski-Doo every year with that. Most northerners must work very hard to make ends meet. They have little disposal income to spend on anything but the barest necessities. Some 40 per cent of individuals filing 1978 income tax returns in settlements in Nunatsiaq, which is my riding, will not even earn enough money in one year to cover the cost of purchasing a $4,000 or $5,000 snowmobile-yet they must have one for hunting. Thus they incur a debt.
Hunters make an invaluable contribution to the health and well-being of their communities but they do not enjoy any tax benefits. In principle, they should be allowed to deduct expenses and claim capital depreciation allowances, just as individuals in the farming and fishing sectors do and, moreover, as the major oil companies do when they explore in the north for oil and gas. However, hunting is not a profit-making business since the meat product is rarely sold and the price of furs is minimal. I will add here that there is a study under way at the present time by the Inuit Development Corporation called the inter-settlement trade study in which the marketability of northern food is being examined to see whether it is marketable in the south and in other northern countries such as Greenland and Alaska.
Few people who are not employed full-time as wage-earners pay taxes. Therefore, a tax credit should be refundable-the base line is a tax credit.
Without going much further, I hope that the motion now before the House will receive the support of all three parties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must commend the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) for the very real concern he shows for the people in his riding and for the people of the north generally. I appreciate the motion put forward by the hon. member.
The federal government and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development particularly is indeed sensitive to the significance of renewable resources and the wellbeing of northerners. We are concerned about the high costs in the north. However, the motion does not appear to provide an answer to either problem. Obviously, the motion intends to resolve problems being encountered by northern residents who no doubt are in need of assistance of some type. After examining the motion, however, I have come to the conclusion that the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act would do little, if anything, to assist the type of people who would be eligible.
The motion proposes to give income tax credits for the purchase of hunting implements to those persons who hunt to provide a substantial portion of their food supply and whose livelihood is hunting. The first question I would ask is why income tax credits should be allowed only to people located in the Northwest Territories, Labrador and Arctic Quebec? It seems to me that there must be residents in the Yukon, particularly natives, who have the same problem as do those living in the area included in the motion. For that matter, I am sure that the same can be said of the residents of the northern parts of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario. The resolution should have been addressed to those people as well.
I do not wish to dwell any longer on the many obvious difficulties which would be encountered in determining the eligibility of applicants for the income tax credits that the hon. member for Nunatsiaq proposes. Adding to the confusion, would be the need for defining such terms as "a substantial portion" and "hunting implements". Then, there would be the problem of determining if an applicant did, in fact, depend on hunting for a substantial portion of his food supply. How and by whom would this be done? These are only a few of the problems which would be encountered in the operation of the proposed income tax credit program. Such a program could become an administrative nightmare. Surely we would not want to complicate the lives of northerners any more than we are now doing, as some members of the opposition have told us many times before.
As I said earlier, the intent of the motion is very praiseworthy but I would object to the proposed means, to the utilization of tax credits. This would do little, if anything, in the way of providing assistance to those with the greatest need.
Perhaps we should review the number of programs which provide assistance to trappers and hunters. I understand that at the territorial level, for example, the government of the Northwest Territories is implementing a program in 1981-82 which would provide grants to subsidize the cost of gasoline to trappers. Those hunters who also trap will benefit. As well,
March 16, 1981

half a million dollars is being provided to assist groups and individuals who wish to live off the land under the outpost camp program of the territorial government.
Furthermore, in discussing northern concerns with the president of the Metis Association of the Northwest Territories, I was informed that there is no federal sales tax on gasoline which is used by hunters and trappers. There is also no sales tax on outboard motors. I suggest that these measures directly assist those whom the hon. member had in mind when he drafted his motion.
At the federal level, again, I point out that there are special ARDA programs geared specifically to Indians and Inuit individuals or groups which provide a large amount of financial assistance. For example, the Rae band received $125,000 assistance under this special program two years ago. I should add that all hunters and trappers associations can benefit from the special ARDA program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The programs I have just mentioned are tailored to the particular needs of Canadians living in the north. If these programs are not functioning properly and if they are not benefiting those whom they should, then I suggest that we review them in order that we may improve on the delivery of the programs to all those who could take advantage of them.
My colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans), will no doubt address the matter of the remission order on the taxation of northern benefits, which has been extended throughout 1981, to allow the Department of Finance the opportunity to develop a reasonable policy on this very important matter. The member for Nunatsiaq may rightly point out that this remission order benefits only the white government employees who are given housing and transportations subsidies. However, I am certain the Department of Finance is examining the question with a view to providing a benefit which will be equitable for all northerners, white and native alike. I further encourage the member for Nunatsiaq to make his views on this policy known to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
In conclusion, we feel the intent of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq has very good merit. However, we do feel that the method suggested would be far too cumbersome and involved, in terms of developing definitions of who should benefit and who depends on hunting for his or her food supply. Again I would ask, to what parts of Canada would the proposal apply? Should it be limited to the areas he has mentioned, or should it be enlarged to apply to all of the country?
We believe that what should be done is to examine in detail the existing programs and try to improve delivery, and if necessary expand the base of funding so that all people who should benefit from those programs receive those benefits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome any opportunity which presents itself in the House to
Income Tax
discuss this crucial important question of the hardship of the northern people, as highlighted in the motion of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar). I naturally speak in support of the motion. I want to congratulate him for taking the initiative of adding this component to the debate, namely, the prospect of providing tax benefits for the purchase and use of hunting implements, hunting being such an important industry, not only to individual families in the north, but also to the economy in general.
I listened with keen interest and some surprise-although one should not be surprised-to the comments of the official speaker of the government in response to this motion. He said that the government is sensitive to the needs of the north and is very much concerned with the high cost of living in the north. This is true. As has been pointed out, there are many federal civil servants living in the north. In fact, there is one federal civil servant for every three northerners.
The government has recognized that there are difficulties in the north and that it is costly to live there, but these difficulties are only recognized when they affect civil servants who are working for the federal government. They have not been recognized in relation to anyone else.
The hon. member made reference to the concern of the government regarding these northern benefits which are only paid to people who happen to work for the federal government. Some large corporations also must pay northern benefits in order to attract people, because it is simply not possible to live and work in the north without some kind of tax relief or subsidy. That is what the government is sensitive about and understand-that it is difficult for bureaucrats to go north, particularly when they can obtain postings elsewhere in Canada. If it is costly and difficult for bureaucrats who work for the federal government, to live in the north, would hon. members not agree that it is equally costly for every other Canadian who lives there?
I published a report just a couple of months ago which points out that if you used no other criteria to help northerners cope with the high cost of living, the difficulties associated with transportation, isolation and so on than those already used by the federal government to compensate its civil servants, it can be established that northerners-and I am including the north of the mid-Canada section of the province-pay $470 million too much in income tax every year. There is no provision in the Income Tax Act to allow for the taxable earnings of these northern benefits. The government has sort of overlooked that.
During the short period of time there was a Conservative government, bureaucrats decided that it would be a good time to tax these northern benefits. Then it was decided that there should be a remission order for a year. This has now been extended, as the hon. member rightly says, to 1981 during which time the government intends to take a very serious look at amending the Income Tax Act to deal adequately with these northern benefits.
I expect there will be a change in the Income Tax Act which will allow for tax free earnings of certain benefits in the north.

March 16, 1981
Income Tax
What that will mean is that tax credits will only accrue to those people in the north who happen to work for large and rich mining companies, or in the lucrative energy sector, or who are federal buraucrats; the rest of the northerners will continue to be second-class citizens. That is simply not good enough.
The Income Tax Act is basically arranged so that every citizen contributes to the economy and operation of this country in accordance with his ability. In other words, one pays income tax in accordance with one's ability to pay. As the hon. member for Nunatsiaq correctly pointed out, people living north of 60 and in the northern part of the provinces pay much less income tax than anyone else in Canada.
The hon. member referred to the price of some of these implements. In some cases, northerners probably pay double what the average Canadian would pay for a Ski-Doo or for a rifle because of freight and delivery costs added to goods shipped to northern consumers. It is common to pay $2 for a gallon of gasoline even in the northern part of the province. I know a place in British Columbia where a gallon of gasoline costs $5. The native people that I represent here use these implements to go out and earn their livelihood, because, as the hon. member said, they cannot buy sufficient and adequate nutritious food for their children.
When I raised this question in the House with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), he asked me to give him names. I would have no difficulty compiling a list of names of people I know who live in my constituency in the province of British Columbia and find it difficult to feed their children and must supplement their food by hunting.
It is generally understood that any money required to buy food, shelter and clothing should not be taxable. That is why we have personal exemptions. However, to a northerner, purchase of these hunting implements is essential because they hunt to provide food, and make clothing from pelts.
A litre of milk in Pond Inlet costs $3.60. In early February this year, two kilograms of sugar cost $6.13 in Pelly Bay. A can of apple juice sold for $4.69. A can of apple sauce costs 49 cents in Edmonton but $ 1.74 in this northern community. The manager of the only store in that community estimated that it now costs $1,526.70 to provide balanced meals for a family of seven for just one month. It is no wonder that those northerners must supplement their foodstuffs by hunting. This becomes even more difficult as they must purchase these implements. As well, they must pay for gasoline and repairs, to maintain them.
The government says it is sensitive to and understands the problems in the north. The parliamentary secretary criticizes the hon. member for Nunatsiaq for not including the Yukon and the northern parts of the provinces in this motion. I would like to do this as well and bring a more universal approach in helping northerners. Even a small step such as the hon. member for Nunatsiaq has suggested would help.
I would like a universal program such as that found in Australia, where there are three different tax zones and a high
cost of living; the living differentials are considered. If I could again use the criteria the federal government uses to compensate its civil servants, people north of 60 would not pay any income tax up to an income of $30,000; and I dare say there are hardly any native people in the north who earn that income. That would be a more universal approach. As well, it would be an incentive which would accrue not only to federal civil servants or employees of large corporations but to all northerners.
This debate is not about my tax proposal, which ministers over there keep telling me is part of a study going on right now in the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Finance and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, it is about a proposal which the hon. member for Nunatsiaq has laid before us.
I would strongly urge all members in this House to give this matter serious consideration and approval. It is a small step toward what I consider is a more universal approach. It will certainly go a long way toward helping some of those people to whom the hon. member for Nunatsiaq made reference, those who have to supplement their own food needs and incomes by hunting so as to overcome some of the incredible burdens placed on northerners as a result of isolation and a harsh environment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tax benefit proposed by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) in his motion would have a very limited impact. In fact, only full-time hunters would stand to gain anything. According to the motion, those are the people "who hunt in order to provide a substantial portion of their food supply and whose livelihood is hunting." So this would apply only to fulltime hunters in the north, namely the Northwest Territories, Labrador and Arctic Quebec. Therefore, hunters residing elsewhere in Canada are not included. In other words, all other hunters in the rest of Canada would be eliminated, leaving only those in the areas I have just mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, that exclusion may be quite justified if we bear in mind the exceptional living conditions of northern residents, and you can be sure that I do not envy them. Still I find it hard to understand why other northern residents would be excluded under this measure, those who earn a living otherwise than by hunting. Most of the other people who live in the north are affected as well by the high cost of living due to the economic difficulties resulting from remoteness, the extremely cold climate, the high cost of transportation and all the other economic problems related to life in the north. I will come back to that question a little bit later, but for now I would like to speak about the income tax issue raised in the motion.
March 16, 1981

First, I wonder if the existing provisions of the Income Tax Act are not adequate under the circumstances. The motion relates to people who hunt for a living and earn enough money to have to file an income tax return. Mr. Speaker, the existing income tax legislation allows those hunters to deduct not only the cost of hunting gear but other expenditures as well, such as ammunition, fuel and special equipment necessary to live off hunting. Naturally, it does not apply to people who now and then go hunting in their leisure time, or who want to taste venison. I do not believe either that it was the suggestion of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq. As things now stand, Mr. Speaker, hunters are allowed to deduct their expenses much in the same way as other self-employed Canadians, including farmers, Fishermen and others in various professions. However, the motion refers to income tax credits rather than a simple tax deduction for the cost of hunting implements. I entertain serious doubts as to whether income tax credits would be the correct approach under such circumstances.
First of all, excluding the child income tax credit, tax credits are especially appropriate for industrial development; thanks to them, a taxpayer can offset in part or in whole his investment expenditures and his tax obligations. It is indeed through tax credits that the federal treasury provides direct assistance to spur investments in plants and equipment with a view to promoting industrial growth, creating new jobs, improving efficiency and boosting productivity. I do not think that hunting can be included in that type of industrial activity.
Mr. Speaker, before supporting a tax credit for hunting implements we should perhaps recognize that such a measure would lead to an increase in hunting. Now is that what we want? Is that what Inuit and Indians in the north really want? Could the wildlife in that area sustain such an increase in hunting? Mr. Speaker, as I said before, this proposal would benefit only one category of northerners, hunters. While recognizing the importance of hunting, especially as an essential part of the livelihood of northerners, I think we must also consider the situation which confronts other residents in the area.
The specific economic hardships that are a fact of life in the north necessarily increase the cost of living for all people in that area. I think we should consider more general approaches that the government could take to ease the economic and social conditions in which those people work and live. I am thinking, for example, Mr. Speaker, of the important role the government plays in providing such services as transportation, communication, health care, environmental protection, housing and social services, to name but a few.
We are all aware of the cutbacks the government was forced to make, but if there were some additional funds to be allocated to northern development, would it not be better to try to improve general services rather than to provide the type of tax incentive suggested in this motion? Mr. Speaker, we should also mention that northerners in general can take
Income Tax
advantage of some work related tax breaks; for example, the housing subsidies that some northern employers provide their employees with. Under the Income Tax Act, such special benefits and allowances would be taxable, which means that this rule is intended to prevent income tax evasion. However, in northern Canada, such allowances are said to be essential to attract workers.
Because of this, Mr. Speaker, the government passed last June a rebate order to exempt for income tax purposes subsidized houses, low-cost housing, as well as travel assistance granted by northern employers for holiday purposes or medical reasons. This debate order which dates back to 1978 will remain in effect until 1981. It is a temporary measure which will give enough time to the government to develop a policy aimed at bringing about a reasonable solution to this difficult and complex problem. Mr. Speaker, we should be considering more important matters, such as the extent and impact of government programs and services in northern Canada and the effect of certain taxation policies. These are the matters which will have the greatest long-term effect on social and economic northern development. In these circumstances, I cannot support such a motion even though the motives of the hon. member are very laudable in view of the very hard and difficult life of the people in northern Canada. Once again, and for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my support to this motion. I find it difficult to follow the arguments coming from the government side. The last speaker mentioned that this would benefit certain groups. The Income Tax Act is full of benefits for certain groups. Therefore, this will not be a precedent.
Insurance agents are part of a special group. They can deduct their expenses for business trips, office equipment and entertainment from their profits. It is quite legal. Farmers are also part of a special group. They can depreciate, over a number of years, the cost of a combine and, in fact, a home which they may build. Therefore, I do not accept the argument that this will benefit a special group.
A few years ago, it was said it would be too difficult to handle a tax credit for children. It has turned out not to be difficult at all. All one has to do is prove that he has children. I have never received an objection from a constituent complaining that he must prove he has children in order to get the tax credit.
Bachelors are not part of that special group and, quite properly, cannot apply for the tax credit. It is only for those who have children, have had to pay the cost of raising them, who get the special tax credit. I commend the government for that type of legislation because the future of this country depends on our boys and girls.

March 16, 1981
Income Tax
I suggest that those in the north who earn the major part of their living do so under the most adverse conditions. It would not be difficult for a northern hunter to prove he has purchased a rifle. He could produce it if necessary. The same applies to a snowmobile or proper clothing. These are essentials. A hunter adds to the net worth of this country. He is producing, not taking away. If we would only accept the idea that those who produce should be encouraged, we would have a lot more production and fewer unemployed.
We hear a lot of talk about inflation and rising interest rates, which puts people out of work. Increasing production would be a better way of fighting inflation. The more production, the less inflation because inflation is too many dollars chasing too few goods. We always attack the problem from one end. Let us increase production which would increase the net worth of this country.
Other people in that category include those in the coal or ore mines. I was raised in a coalmining town. My father and brothers were miners. I saw the toll it takes in human life, working in the bosom of the earth, with no sunshine, sometimes on their hands and knees lifting the coal in smoky conditions. They are paid by the ton.
I can take you to coal mining towns in Alberta, and others can probably do the same in Ontario and the maritimes, and show you how the health of the people has deteriorated after having spent their lives producing coal, lead, zinc or whatever the ore happened to be. We should find ways and means to help increase the production and thus fight inflation.
When we have this type of motion which encourages production and asks for an incentive, an encouragement, we should not say it cannot be done, but look to see how we can assist. This bill should be sent to committee, where we could hear from experts on the north, including the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar). We could find ways and means to help them and increase production. That is why we were elected to this place.
Rather than looking for reasons why we should not do something, we should change our attitude to one that is more positive. I urge members on the government side to not defeat this because of one or two obstacles. It will not cost the government anything to send this to committee where it can be considered. If sound reasons are advanced why this cannot be done, I am sure the hon. member for Nunatsiaq would be the first to accept that.
I am satisfied that we can find ways to increase the production and therefore the wealth of this country. It would give those people doing this type of work, under conditions most people would not even consider, some encouragement and incentive to continue. I urge hon. members to send this to committee where it can be discussed in detail. If there are sound reasons why it cannot be done, it can be defeated there. Let us not throw it out here because there may be one or two obstacles in the way of what we want to do.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) for introducing
this motion to the House. It is one that I basically support. There is no question that the people not only living in the two territories but in the areas close to the territorial boundaries in the provinces are in need of every possible break from the income tax people, every possible fiscal break we can give them.
We think costs have been escalating in the south. This afternoon we heard the hon. member for Nunatsiaq indicate the astronomical increases there have been in the cost of living for those in the territories and the northern parts of many of our provinces. We should do our best to give them the tax advantages that will allow them to make a dent in the continually increasing cost of living which, while we are all subjected to it, seems to affect them in an even more severe way. The idea of giving income tax credits on the purchase of hunting implements may well be a means whereby this can be achieved. There may be other methods as well, and it seems to me we should be looking at this entire question carefully. How can we make aspects of northern livelihood a more important part of the economy up there; how we can encourage, for example, not only by these methods but by others having to do with conservation and a better organization of the management of animal life in these territories, how can we encourage a more effective harvesting of the animal life for the benefit of the people living in those areas.
In parts of the north there is literally a tremendous potential for an increase in the animal harvest. The Lancaster Sound area the hon. member for Nunatsiaq referred to has the potential to become almost a granary of the north because it has such a rich marine life base and the land animals associated with this bountiful marine life are rich in number and potential as well. These rich pockets of animal life in the north, and I understand there are several of them, have the potential to be exploited for the benefit of the local population and we should be doing our best to encourage that, both by setting up the kind of conservation framework that will allow for proper management and more effective harvesting. With proper planning I am convinced this can be done.
I would suggest there are perhaps other methods of bringing the costs of some of these items down for people living in the north. I know the co-operative movement is active in the north but it seems to me there must be better ways of reducing the cost of these items by using better purchasing methods down here or having some sort of centralized purchasing mechanism here that will allow people in the north to benefit from the lowest possible prices instead of having several middlemen along the way taking a percentage, with the result that prices are two or three times as high as we have to pay.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and I would support an effort to have the subject matter of this motion referred to that committee. It seems to me that by such a reference our committee could look at not only what the hon. member is proposing, but also at some of the other items I mentioned, at
March 16, 1981

what we can do to reduce costs for the people living there and achieve a more useful utilization of the marine and animal resources of the north, for the people concerned.
1 am convinced there is a method of combining capacity with conservation which will result in a maximum harvest and sensible conservation, and do this in a way that will benefit primarily the people of the north, by referring this matter to committee we can look at the question of tax credits as part of the broader question of helping the people of the north and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Nunatsiaq would agree that this suggestion makes sense.
