Air Canada has now stepped aside from its wish to provide this service. I think the time has come for the Minister of Transport to move. No U.S. carrier wants to serve this route, and no Canadian carrier wants to serve this route because their jets are too large for the service required. This route is ideal for a regional airline. It is ideal because of the capacity and willingness regional carriers have shown.
I think the time has come for the minister to speak up for Canada. I think it is time for the minister to speak up for his own constituency. I believe it is time for the minister to speak up on behalf of those governmental, business, professional and other organizations who can see nothing but good in this service. Because there is this interest, I think I have a right to expect that the minister's assistant will say he will move to
March 16, 1981

change the agreement if it is necessary, and he will press upon the people in the United States the importance of allowing Canadians to compete for that right. I hope that will be the answer I shall receive from his parliamentary secretary. I look forward to it tonight with hopeful expectation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-DIRECT AIR SERVICE BETWEEN OTTAWA AND NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) pointed out in the House on March 13, this issue cannot be answered as though there were no air transport agreement between Canada and the United States. The agreement exists, and it gives the United States certain rights which we have to respect, in the same way as we expect the United States to respect Canada's rights. In particular, the agreement gives a U.S. carrier the right to operate between New York and Ottawa.
On this basis, it is difficult to see why the United States would agree to allow a Canadian carrier to operate this route until it had been shown that no U.S. carrier is interested. Expressed in a different way, the U.S. has first right of refusal to that route.
Recognizing this reality, the minister urged the U.S. authorities to determine as quickly as possible whether there was, in fact, any U.S. carrier interested in serving the route. If not, then there would be a strong presumption that the U.S. would agree to a Canadian carrier being granted the right to operate an Ottawa to New York service. In that case, if the CTC saw fit to licence either First Air or Air Atonabee, that carrier would be free, immediately thereafter, to seek the same authority from the U.S. Civil Aeronautics Board, which it must do before it can begin service.
The approach the minister has been following is the only practical one, given Canada's legal obligations. It certainly promises faster results than any approach, such as the one apparently being suggested by the hon. member which would ignore these obligations.

Mr. Speaker, on January 20 last I raised a matter with respect to the Grange commission report which had been delivered to hon. members the day before, January 19. The report was a result of a train accident which took place in the city of Mississauga on November 10, 1979, at 10.15 p.m. wherein a CPR train travelling on the main CPR line through Mississauga at 50 or 60 miles an hour derailed because of a hot box.
The commission to look into that accident was formulated as a result of a unanimous motion in this House on November 12 which was followed up by questions in the transport committee on November 13. On November 13 the Canadian Transport Commission said it would inquire into its own faults. As a result of that hearing before the transport committee, it became apparent that the CTC had been acting as a sleeping policeman.
Adjournment Debate
The CTC had been involved in a similar inquiry in 1971. In that inquiry a number of recommendations were made with respect to safety and the carriage of dangerous goods. Being a sleeping policeman, the CTC went back to sleep and did nothing.
If the Canadian Transport Commission had not gone back to sleep the evacuation of the city of Mississauga would not have occurred. Indeed, the accident probably would not have occurred. As the minister suggested in a response to me, the CTC was very interested in relation to the economic viability in connection with the existing considerations. He said maybe the time had come to change that view of economic considerations.
The accident in Mississauga occurred partly and perhaps largely because the Canadian Transport Commission, which is in charge of rail safety under the Railway Act, was a sleeping policeman. It refused to recognize that chlorine was a dangerous substance, more than just a compressed gas, and refused to recognize the explosive properties of propane. It refused to understand the dangerous properties of caustic soda.
The train which sped through Mississauga at 10.15 p.m. November 10 developed a hot box, another subject of CTC inquiries dating back many years. In particular, the 1971 inquiry was not looked at. When you look at the recommendations of Mr. Justice Grange you will see it says: The CTC or Transport Canada shall; the CTC should require; the CTC should require an immediate trial by railways of the following; the CTC should implement its intention expressed in Glacier, British Columbia. Recommendation after recommendation says the CTC should have done, it should have acquired, it should have performed.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), defender of bureaucracy, defender of ineptitude, sits back and says: Well, these things happen; perhaps it was a question of the times, but refuses to come to grips with the problems of rail safety. All of my constituents, residents of Mississauga, were evacuated, most for an entire seven days, and the CTC was partly, indeed largely, responsible. Had the organization we entrusted in the Railway Act defended rail safety, brought the red book up to snuff, a book containing a set of rules prepared by the American Railway Association back in 1919 and hardly amended since, had they paid attention to the security of people in built-up areas, then perhaps the Mississauga derailment might not have occurred. The Grange Commission points that out seriously. We have not yet had action by this minister even though he had the report from the Grange Commission at least six weeks before it was in the hands of Members of Parliament. The replies I received from the minister on January 20, sir, indicate a Minister of Transport who is not prepared to do his job.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be afforded the opportunity to inform the House of the recent initiatives of the Canadian Transport Commission in the field of rail safety.
8310

March 16, 1981
Adjournment Debate
I would particularly like to highlight recent CTC activities in five major areas related to the movement of dangerous goods.
First, on November 27, 1979, an order was issued to each railway company under the committee's jurisdiction requiring that tank car shipments be marshalled so that flammable compressed gases are separated from tank car shipments of chlorine, anhydrous ammonia or sulphur dioxide by at least five rail cars containing no dangerous commodities. Second, two years ago, CTC instigated a tank car retrofit program that is still in progress. Equipment to be retrofitted includes double shelf couplers, head shields, bottom fitting protection, and thermal protection, precisely the equipment recommended by Judge Grange in his recent report. Third, the commission has intensified its inspection program for dangerous commodity storage facilities located on railway rights of way. As a direct result of this program, two such storage installations in Alberta have been closed in the last year. Fourth, the CTC has instigated a review of dangerous commodity movements in various sections of the country. Last, the commission has issued a series of regulations affecting the "red book" regulations, life saving devices, the contents of shipping documents, and tank car outage requirements.
The CTC also upgraded its response to rail accidents in three specific ways. First, the railways have been required to instigate a telephone alert system to ensure that all major accidents are immediately reported to the commission. Second, the CTC has appointed a commissioner to investigate major accidents on site, to recommend interim and long-term measures which would enhance safety, and to hold public inquiries when warranted, in the aftermath of accidents. Third, the commission is now purchasing protective clothing and updated hazard-detecting equipment for its staff for use at accident scenes.
Judge Grange restricted his inquiry, according to his mandate, to "the lessons from Mississauga". The Canadian Transport Commission obviously cannot take such a limited view. To respond to the need for greater safety we cannot afford to focus all our attention on Mississauga or any other single accident to the exclusion of other equally important safety factors.
Finally, I should like to address the question of resources available to the commission. A submission is now at Treasury Board seeking an additional 31 person-years in respect of rail safety. I trust that Treasury Board will view this submission favourably so that Canadian Transport Commission rail safety responsibilities may be enhanced to a greater degree.
These points demonstrate that the Canadian Transport Commission is taking its rail safety responsibilities seriously and that the existing programs, combined with the response to the Grange inquiry, will ensure that Canadians continue to have a safe and efficient rail transportation system.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT-SUGGESTED DISCUSSION OF ACID RAIN PRECIPITATION IN CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS
THE ENVIRONMENT-SUGGESTED DISCUSSION OF ACID RAIN PRECIPITATION IN CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what specific proposals he would be making to President Reagan concerning the acid rain crisis while the latter was visiting Ottawa. The Prime Minister responded that the issue would be discussed but that he would not use any threat in order to conclude an agreement on trans-boundary air pollution.
In his remarks the President of the United States alluded only briefly to the acid rain problem, and to this date there have been no specific concrete proposals made by either country as the result of the President's visit. In other words, we will apparently continue to discuss, to debate, to study and to procrastinate while the most critical environmental hazard continues to destroy our lakes and rivers, our crops and our forests.
Acid precipitation is produced in both Canada and the United States, but the United States dumps four times as much S02 on Canada as we dump on the United States. In Canada, fairly successful attempts have been made to reduce acid rain in recent years. For example, in the Sudbury basin Inco Metals Limited, the largest single acid rain polluter in North America, has reduced its emissions by 80 per cent in the last ten years. Ontario Hydro has been ordered to reduce its fallout by 50 per cent. Steps are being taken in Alberta to prevent acid rain from becoming an environmental problem.
In the United States, regrettably, the picture is very different. To date there has been no appreciable reduction in acid rain whatsoever. Worse still, with the vast conversion in that country to coal-fired electrical generating plants in the northeast, acid rain will increase substantially in the near future, further damaging Canada's environment, particularly in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes.
Ontario has already lost or is about to lose 4,000 lakes, and within ten years, we are told by the scientific community, some 45,000 lakes in Ontario will die if nothing is done now. We cannot afford to wait while an anti-environmentalist U.S. President dithers.
We cannot afford to continue to be polite and continue to negotiate as friends and neighbours if those friends are ignorant and complacent and for political reasons their government has committed itself to go easy on environmental issues for purely economic reasons.
We have a fairly good idea of the cost of cleaning up trans-boundary pollution. It is in the billions of dollars. But to wait will cost infinitely more, and if we wait too long no amount of money will repair the damage.
In my remarks to the Prime Minister last week I suggested that if the United States could not be persuaded to conclude a treaty to reduce and eliminate acid rain precipitation, then Canada should threaten to cut off hydroelectric power to that country. This would be a very drastic measure to take, and I admit that, but I am convinced this kind of threat is the only effective way to get action on this political issue. How else
March 16, 1981

does one convince an ignorant and apathetic people and its foot-dragging President to resolve an issue of this magnitude?
The province of Ontario recently launched a legal suit against some 18 power plants in the United States which are converting to coal from oil. This is a long and costly process. What is needed at this time is political action. We already have a memorandum of intent, signed on August 5, 1980. We must proceed to a strong treaty immediately.
There is already overwhelming scientific evidence concerning the critical damage caused by acid rain. There is also well documented evidence as to its sources. We also have the technological know-how to stop it. What we do not have is a Prime Minister with the courage to tell the U.S. that enough is enough. In other words, we do not have a prime minister with the courage to tell President Reagan that his country has to stop killing ours.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT-SUGGESTED DISCUSSION OF ACID RAIN PRECIPITATION IN CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me thank my good friend, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), for allowing this opportunity to have this rather urgent subject aired once again. I believe, as I understand he believes, that a good part of the acid rain issue, both in the United States and in Canada, is the lack of awareness and public profile it commands at present. That is especially true in the United States. I share his concern and I welcome the opportunity to endorse the sentiments he has expressed in so far as those sentiments relate to the depth of his concern. I do not share his sentiments as to the strategies which he has advocated, and I shall take a moment of the time of the House to indicate why I do not share his proposed strategies.
Last week, when the President of the U.S. was here, Mr. Reagan, the Prime Minister, (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) took advantage of the opportunity to state very clearly our concerns here in Canada
Adjournment Debate
over acid rain and the need for continued co-operation and progress under the memorandum of intent to which the hon. member for Brant has referred this evening. President Reagan gave his assurance at those meetings last week to the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment that his administration will continue to support the activities of the Canada-U.S. work groups which were formed under the annex to the memorandum of intent last August. Indeed, the interim report of these groups was released on February 13, and further reports can be expected in mid-1981 and early 1982. The reports of these work groups will be the foundation for the negotiation which we hope will begin within the next few months, by June of this year it is hoped.
The forecast of increased emissions of sulphur dioxide in the United States, referred to by the hon. member for Brant in an earlier question on this subject, is speculative at this point. It is speculative in the sense that it assumes no control action will be taken by the United States government in respect of existing sources, nor for those thermal power plants which are slated to be converted from oil to coal. I believe it would be counterproductive for us to enter into negotiations with the U.S. on the basis of such an assumption. It would be equally inopportune, I submit, to begin brandishing the threat of sanctions against the United States before the negotiations even begin.
Finally, contrary to what the hon. member has suggested, we have no indication at this time that the U.S. cannot be persuaded to conclude an agreement. Indeed, the indications right now are quite to the contrary. They are pursuing, in good faith, their work jointly with us in the Canada-U.S. work groups.
